## Chronic kidney disease stages 4-5: Patient management
Fiona Murphy is Lecturer and Renal Educational Facilitator, School of Nursing and Midwifery, Trinity College Dublin, 24 D'Olier Street, Dublin 2, Ireland; Gobnait Byrne is Lecturer, School of Nursing and Midwifery, Trinity College Dublin. Email : fi ona.murphy@tcd.ie

T his is the third in a series of four articles which will discuss the cardiovascular implications within renal care. Th e aims of these articles are to highlight the important role that renal dysfunction plays in the care of cardiac patients. Th e fi rst article addressed acute kidney injury and its impact on cardiac patients (Byrne and Murphy, 2008). Th e second article explored the role of chronic kidney disease (CKD) stages 1 to 3 and its close interrelationship with cardiovascular disease (CVD) (Murphy and Byrne, 2009). Th is third article in this series will explore CKD stages 4 to 5, while the fi nal article will develop further the cardiac implications of renal replacement therapies.

Th is article will discuss the many physical symptoms which impact on individuals at CKD stages 4 to 5 including hypertension, dyslipidaemia, anaemia, potassium disorders, mineral and bone disorder, metabolic acidosis, gastrointestinal and dermatological disorders ( Figure 1 ). It is vital that patients are prepared for renal replacement therapies at CKD stage 5 which include timely education including nutritional support along with psychological and social support.

Th e recent National Institute for Health and Clinical Excellence (NICE) guidelines identify that an average of

30% of people with advanced kidney disease are referred late to renal services from both primary and secondary care resulting in increased mortality and morbidity (National Collaborating Centre for Chronic Conditions (NCC-CC, 2008). Over 2% of the total NHS budget is spent on patients requiring renal replacement therapies. Patients at stage 4 and 5 CKD should therefore be referred for specialist assessment (with or without diabetes) (NCC-CC, 2008) (see Table 1 ).

Th e NICE guidelines (NCC-CC, 2008) further highlight that measures should be taken to identify progressive CKD. Th is includes obtaining a minimum of three estimated glomerular fi ltration rate (eGFR) measurements over a period of not less than 90 days. In individuals with a new result of a reduced eGFR, this eGFR should be repeated within a two-week timeframe to rule out causes of acute deterioration of GFR such as acute kidney injury or the instigation of a drug regime of angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors or angiotensin receptor blockers (ARBs).

## Abstract
Chronic kidney disease (CKD) is classifi ed into fi ve stages with stages 1 to 3 identifi ed as early CKD. This disease advances further in stage 4, while in stage 5 patients require renal replacement therapy (dialysis and transplantation) to survive. The risk factors for cardiovascular disease (CVD) are also the risk factors for CKD, while CKD is itself a key risk factor for CVD. A high proportion of patients with CKD will die from CVD. The nursing care of patients with stages 4-5 CKD includes the management of the many physical symptoms associated with these late stages such as hypertension, dyslipidaemia, anaemia, potassium disorders, mineral and bone disorder, metabolic acidosis, gastrointestinal and dermatological disorders. It is vital that patients are prepared for renal replacement therapies at CKD stage 5 which include timely education including nutritional support along with psychological and social support.

It is important to pay particular attention to those individuals in whom a reduction in GFR continues at a rate which would (extrapolating the current pace of decline) lead to them needing renal replacement therapy within their lifespan (NCC-CC, 2008).

CVD remains the most frequent source of death in patients with end-stage renal disease (ESRD), and CKD patients are most likely to die from CVD than are expected to advance to ESRD. Th ere is overwhelming scientifi c evidence to support the facts that proteinuria and decreased GFR are independent risk factors for CVD ( Figure 2 ). Th e CKD population has an increased prevalence of traditional cardiovascular risk factors such as diabetes, hypertension, and dyslipidaemia (Chonchol and Spiegel, 2009) (see Figure 3 for traditional and non-traditional risk factors associated with CKD).

## Hypertension
It is vital that hypertension is treated to slow the downward spiral of CKD. Th ere are many benefi ts with regards reducing blood pressure, including the risk of a stroke being decreased by 35-40%, the risk of a myocardial infarction (MI) being decreased by 20-5% and the risk of heart failure decreasing by 50% (Benavente et al, 2008a). NICE guidelines (NCC-CC, 2008) recommend aiming to keep the systolic blood pressure below 140 mmHg (target range 120-139 mmHg) with the diastolic blood pressure below 90 mmHg for individuals with CKD. For those patients with CKD and diabetes and those that have an albumin creatinine ratio (ACR) of 70 mg/mmol or more, the recommendation is to keep the systolic blood pressure below 130 mmHg (target range 120-129 mmHg) and the diastolic blood pressure below 80 mmHg.

Th e fi rst choice of antihypertensive drugs should be ACE inhibitors followed by ARBs if the ACE inhibitors are not tolerated (NCC-CC, 2008). Th ese medications reduce systemic blood pressure and also reduce intraglomerular pressure thereby protecting the kidneys from more severe disease progression. Both the serum creatinine and potassium should be monitored within 1 to 2 weeks aft er commencing a patient on an ACE inhibitor or an ARB. It may be necessary to repeat this monitoring with dose increases, especially in individuals more at risk of hyperkalaemia (Young, 2008).

Th e role of the nurse is paramount here through health promotion. Lifestyle modifi cations for patients to manage hypertension include weight reduction, dietary sodium reduction, physical activity and moderations of alcohol consumption (Benavente et al, 2008a). Patients should be educated regarding the importance of recording blood pressure monitoring and be encouraged to carry out blood pressure monitoring at home (Young, 2008).

## Dyslipidaemia
Dyslipidaemia can occur early in CKD and can deteriorate as the overall kidney function declines which is the case at stages 4 to 5 CKD. Th ere are various contributing factors including the presence of diabetes, proteinuria and the level of kidney function. As patients with CKD are at the highest risk for CVD, it is wise to treat dyslipidaemia aggressively (Benavente et al, 2008a). However, the NICE

Figure 2. Some postulated pathophysiological links between CKD and increased CVD risk (Burrows and Muller, 2007)

<!-- image -->

guidelines (NCC-CC, 2008) suggest that the use of statin therapy for the primary prevention of CVD in individuals with CKD should not diff er from its use in individuals without CKD and should be refl ected by existing risk tables for individuals with and without diabetes. Th ey further identify that statins should be off ered to individuals with CKD for the secondary prevention of CVD irrespective of baseline lipid values. Adil and Aslam (2009) assert that patients with CKD should generally receive a statin if they have elevated levels of low density lipoprotein (LDL) if dietary manipulation is unsuccessful aft er 3 months.

## Potassium disorders
Th e ability of the kidneys to maintain potassium at near normal levels is usually maintained until the GFR falls to less than 20-25 ml/minute or individuals become oliguric. Hyperkalaemia can occur in CKD as a result of nonadherence to dietary restrictions, infection, constipation, following episodes of acute illness, haemorrhage, blood transfusion and medications such as ACE inhibitors, betablockers, ARBs, potassium-sparing diuretics and nonsteroidal anti-infl ammatory drugs (NSAIDs).

It can be aggravated also by salt and water depletion, an extracellular shift of potassium which can occur in chronic metabolic acidosis or a lack of insulin. Th e management of hyperkalaemia conservatively includes attention to diet such as the avoidance of potassium-rich foods such as chocolate, bananas and citrus fruits and avoidance of the above mentioned medications.

However, for those patients taking ACE inhibitors or ARBs these should be temporarily stopped or a loop diuretic or oral sodium bicarbonate added to the regime oft en ameliorates hyperkalaemia. Renal replacement therapies such as haemodialysis are indicated in refractory hyperkalaemia (Benavente et al, 2008a; Hurst and Th omas, 2008; Guo and Aslam, 2009).

NICE guidelines recommend that serum calcium, phosphate and PTH concentrations in individuals at stages 4 to 5 CKD should be monitored but the subsequent frequency of monitoring should be determined by the measured values and the clinical circumstances (NCC-CC, 2008). NKF-K/DOQI (2003) advises that PTH, calcium and phosphate should be measured every three months for patients at stage CKD 4, and at stage 5 these bloods should be measured every month.

scribed if dietary reduction is insuffi cient such as sevelamer hydrochloride (renagel). It is important to keep the serum calcium towards the middle or low range of normal, to reduce the risk of vascular calcifi cation. Th e administration of active vitamin D sterol has been associated with improved survival and better cardiovascular outcomes (Pendse and Singh, 2007). Dinwiddie et al (2006) assert that nurses should provide information to patients with regard to CKD MBD (such as that already discussed) along with weight-bearing exercises, fall prevention, and the avoidance of NSAIDs (which are nephrotoxic). Other risk factors should be addressed such as osteoporosis, muscle strength and gait, presence or absence of bone pain and any reduction in movement.

## Metabolic acidosis
Th e ability of the kidneys to eff ectively eliminate the total acid load is reduced with advancing CKD (Young, 2008). Th ere is a decrease in total ammonia excretion which is responsible for acidosis. Th is results in a decreased net hydrogen secretion and a reduction in serum bicarbonate. Th e adverse consequences of this include protein malnutrition, suppression of albumin synthesis. Th ere is also dissolution of bone leading to deterioration uremic osteodystrophy as a result of the net positive acid balance. Early treatment is recommended such as oral bicarbonate therapy, however, care must be taking not to hasten or worsen hypertension with the added sodium intake (Chonchol and Spiegel, 2009). Hurst and Th omas (2008) and Benavente et al (2008a) suggest that the safest method at this stage to control bicarbonate balance is dialysis.

## Gastrointestinal disorders
Anorexia, weight loss, nausea and vomiting, halitosis, a metallic taste in the mouth, hiccups, are frequent fi ndings as the patient advances towards ESRD. Ammonia, which is produced from urea broken down in the gut, acts as an irritant. Th ere is also increased gastric acid secretion from increased release of PTH. Th e side eff ects of some medications like oral phosphate binders and oral iron medication can cause heartburn. Constipation is another potential eff ect, due to a reduced fl uid intake as CKD advances in stages 4 and 5. Overall the individual at these stages can be less physically active and therefore more lethargic and tired (Broscious and Castagnola, 2006; Hurst and Th omas, 2008). Th e role of the nurse is to assess individuals' oral mucous membranes, monitor weight, observe stools for occult blood, monitor breath odour (Broscious and Castagnola, 2006) and to liaise with the renal dietician.

## Dermatological disorders
As CKD advances there is deposition of calcium and phosphorus in the skin, and the sweat glands excrete urea resulting in uraemic pruritis. Other dermatological side eff ects include bleeding and bruising of the skin as a result of platelet defects and capillary permeability, particularly if the patients are constantly scratching. Individuals at stages 4 to 5 may also present with a yellow tinge to their

<!-- image -->

skin due to a combination of hypermelanosis and the deposits of pigments in the skin that are generally excreted by the kidneys. Th ere is antihistamine medication available which should assist with pruritis; however, the long term relief would be the commencement of dialysis (Hurst and Th omas 2008).
